it: When I see your work manipulating fog, I’m reminded of Fujiko Nakaya and E.A.T.'s Pepsi Pavilion at Expo '70 in Osaka. Much like yourselves, Nakaya and E.A.T. were both envisioning new relationships between art, science, nature and engineering. What do you take from that lineage?

What did you take from the lineage of E.A.T. and Fujiko Nakaya?
Nakaya also typically conceals any sign of machinery.

How does showing your machinery differ from Nakaya’s concealment of hers?

Fascinating. I co-wrote a piece with Primavera De Filippi where we argue art has been slowly acquiring the components of life. I think your practice demonstrates this. How does your relationship with objects explain the difference between Studio Swine and A.A.Murakami?

You mentioned ephemeral tech and maybe you can say more about what it can achieve. It’s grounded in an aversion to screens, projections, LEDs and the familiar technological interfaces that dominate art and technology.

You’re having a busy year with eight shows running or opening in 2026: Venice, Basel Unlimited, Copenhagen, Barcelona, Mumbai, Arnhem and two in Seoul, with New Nature opening at Paradise Art Center in September. What does this moment feel like from inside the studio? Is there a thread connecting it all?
